---
title: "Set-up"
subtitle: Setting up the hardware and software for GrandOrgue
---

## Raspberry Pi setup

Raspberry Pi (RPi) devices run Debian-based Raspberry Pi OS. GrandOrgue needs the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS in order to utilize all of the installed RAM (a 32-bit OS would cap the usable RAM at 4 GB, regardless of what is installed in the system.) The 64-bit OS conveniently comes pre-installed on the CanaKit RPi.

Before installing anything, download and install any OS updates:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot
```

GrandOrgue [recommends X11](https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/blob/master/INSTALL.md) to properly handle window sizing and positioning. To switch the display mode:

1. Open a terminal and run `sudo raspi-config`
2. Use the down arrow key to select **Advanced Options**
3. In the next menu, select **Wayland**
4. Select **X11**, then **\<OK\>**
5. Use the right arrow key to select **\<Finish\>** and then **Reboot**

The touch monitor was plug-and-play. Since the RPi 5 only has a single USB-C port, which is used for the power supply, the monitor needed to be connected to the RPi via both HDMI for data and USB for power. I used the HDMI to mini-HDMI cable that came with the RPi and the USB-C to USB-A cable that came with the monitor. The RPi did need to be rebooted after everything was connected for the touch screen to work properly.

## GrandOrgue installation

From the [GrandOrgue releases GitHub](https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases), download the `arm64.deb` architecture package. As of May 2026, the current release was `grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb`. You can also download it directly in the terminal:

```bash
wget https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases/download/3.17.1-1/grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb
```

(Note: `grandorgue` requires **wxWidgets 3.2** and `grandorgue-wx30` requires **wxWidgets 3.0**. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships with wxWidgets 3.2, so the standard `grandorgue` package above is the correct one.)

Install the software using either the downloaded installer or terminal:

```bash
sudo apt install ./grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb
```

You might get a `Permission Denied` warning, but it can be ignored:  

```bash
N: Download is performed unsandboxed as root as file '/home/username/grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb' couldn't be accessed by user '_apt'. - pkgAcquire::Run (13: Permission denied)
```

It is not a fatal error; the application should have installed fine. 

Verify the installation by looking for it in the **Sound & Video** application menu. Launch the program. It should open and load the demo organ.

### MIDI

Next, configure the MIDI hardware:

1. Plug in the Behringer UMC204HD USB audio interface to the RPi via USB and to the keyboard or organ using MIDI cables.
2. Open GrandOrgue and go to **File** → **Preferences** → **Audio**. You should see the UMC204HD listed as an ALSA device. Select it, set the sample rate to 48000 Hz and start with 512 samples per buffer.
3. You can tune the buffer size down later if latency feels sluggish, or up if you hear crackle.
4. Go to **File** → **Preferences** → **MIDI Devices**. The UMC204HD's MIDI ports should appear as ALSA MIDI devices. 
5. Enable the input port. Then load a sample set.

### GrandOrgue configuration

Next, we need to map MIDI channels between GrandOrgue and the instrument.

1. Go to **File** → **Settings** → **MIDI Devices**
2. Under **MIDI output devices**, make sure UNC204HD is selected. Click **OK**.
3. On the virtual pipe organ (VPO) console, right-click a virtual manual to map to.
4. In the box that opens, click **Listen for Event**. Play a key on the keyboard you wish to map to that virtual organ manual.
5. Click **OK**.

To reduce audio lag:

1. **File** → **Settings** → ((Audi))o
2. Set the **Samples per buffer** to 256 or 128 (defaults to 512).

The lower the buffer size, the lower the latency. At 48,000 Hz sample rate, 128 samples per buffer supposedly gives about 2.7 milliseconds of latency, which is completely imperceptible. The tradeoff is that very low buffer sizes can cause audio crackle or dropouts if the RPi can't process audio fast enough. The Pi 5 should, however, be plenty powerful enough to handle 128 samples without trouble, especially with the demo sample set.

Even at 128 samples/buffer, I still noticed a lag, but it was better than when I started. It is possible that some delay is "built in" as the result of the sample recording. This remains to be determined. I am accustomed to old-technology, non-realistic digital organs on which the sound is instantaneous, whereas many pipe organs have a slight (fraction of a second) lag between the time a key is depressed and the sound is actually heard.

### Audio

By default, the VPO plays through the computer speakers -- in this case, the speakers on the touch screen monitor. Much better sound quality can be obtained with better speakers or headphones.

Bluetooth headphones may experience a fairly significant lag in audio. It did for me. Since my old keyboard did not have an Audio In jack, I could not channel the sound back to the keyboard speakers -- which was just as well, because they are not very good either. The best (but not perfect) option was wired headphones plugged into the UNC204HD interface. The only headphones I owned had a 1/8" plug, so I had to use a 1/4"-1/8" adapter to connect them. There was a slight buzz, possibly resulting from the extra connection. It was annoying, but not bad enough to abandon the setup.
